headline: Aura points: the internet's new game of looking cool

sources.title: What is an 'Aura Battle'? Why is everyone suddenly 'Farming Aura' (Hola)
The boy behind the viral 'aura farming' boat racing dance (BBC)
What is 'aura farming'? Gen Z's viral obsession with looking cool (South China Morning Post)
Who is the aura-farming boat kid? (video, CBC Kids News)

chunks.text: Some people just seem cool. They walk into a room and {{come across}} as [[effortlessly]] calm and [[relaxed]]. They {{give off}} an easy, quiet [[confidence]] without trying. On the internet, that [[quality]] now has a name: [[aura]]. Teenagers everywhere talk about gaining and losing [[aura points]], [[imaginary]] [[scores]] for every cool or [[embarrassing]] moment in daily life. The idea began in [[gaming]] culture, and in 2026 it is everywhere.

verbs.correct: To seem a certain way to others
verbs.why: A shy person can come across as unfriendly at first, and a nervous speaker can come across as more confident than he feels. On the internet, some people just come across as effortlessly cool without even trying.

verbs.correct: To produce a feeling or energy
verbs.why: A lit candle gives off a warm light, and a confident person gives off calm energy without saying a word. Teenagers now describe this quality as aura, the feeling someone simply gives off in a room.

chunks.text: The trend exploded thanks to one boy. In 2025, a video went [[viral]]: an eleven-year-old from Indonesia was dancing calmly on the front [[tip]] of a long, narrow racing boat. His relaxed moves {{won over}} millions of viewers, and kids around the world now {{look up to}} him as the king of cool. People joked that he had {{racked up}} more aura points than anyone alive. The joke created a new phrase, [[aura farming]], which even reached a famous dictionary's [[shortlist]] for word of the year.

verbs.correct: To gain someone's support or love
verbs.wrong: To beat someone in a game
verbs.why: A new teacher can win over a whole class within a week, and honest answers can win over even the toughest judges. The boy's calm dance moves won over millions of viewers around the world.
Young players look up to their team captain, and kids often look up to an older sibling or a coach. Now kids around the world look up to this calm eleven-year-old as the king of cool.

verbs.correct: To collect a large number of points
verbs.why: A champion racks up win after win over a long season, and a frequent flyer racks up miles without even noticing. Fans joked that the boy had racked up more aura points than anyone alive.

chunks.text: The rules are simple but strict. When a skater {{pulls off}} a hard [[trick]] perfectly, his aura grows. If he {{messes up}} in front of everyone, the points vanish instantly. And there is a [[twist]]: visible effort is [[fatal]]. People who {{show off}} their new clothes and money usually lose aura, not gain it. True aura belongs to those who {{stand out}} without trying, or at least without letting anyone see the trying. Coolness, the internet has decided, must look [[accidental]].

verbs.why: A skater can pull off a hard trick on the first try, and a team can pull off a surprise win against the odds. In this game, a skater who pulls off a hard trick perfectly watches his aura grow instantly.

verbs.wrong: To win by a small amount
verbs.why: Everyone messes up a name at some point, and a nervous actor can mess up his lines on opening night. If a player messes up in front of everyone here, the aura points disappear right away.

A proud driver shows off a new car around the block, and a student shows off a shiny new trophy at school. Here, people who show off their new clothes or money usually lose points instead of gaining them.

verbs.correct: To be easy to notice among others
verbs.why: A bright red coat can stand out in a gray winter crowd, and a calm voice can stand out in a loud, noisy meeting. True aura belongs to people who stand out without even seeming to try.

chunks.text: This summer, the game turned physical. In parts of Latin America, thousands of people now attend aura battles, live [[contests]] where two players face each other and try to look cooler with every move. At some Mexican events, winners take home [[prizes]] of about 3,000 pesos. Most fans just {{play along}} at home, rating their friends' aura after every party. Meanwhile, [[psychologists]] are not worried. Learning to [[play it cool]], they say, is an old teenage sport. Only the [[scoreboard]] is new.

verbs.correct: To join a game and act your part
verbs.wrong: To stop a game before the end
verbs.why: A parent might play along with a child's pretend game, and a good sport plays along with a joke even when he sees it coming. Most fans simply play along at home, rating each other's aura after every party.

mainIdea.s: Young people online now measure coolness with imaginary aura points, a trend that grew from gaming and one viral boat video. It has even created live contests this year.
mainIdea.why: The article explains aura points, the boy who made aura farming famous, and the aura battles now held in Latin America.

mainIdea.s: Young people are earning real money by collecting coolness points inside a popular phone game. The app pays its calmest players about three thousand pesos every month.
mainIdea.why: Close, but aura points are imaginary. The pesos are prizes at live events in Mexico, not monthly app payments.

mainIdea.s: Doctors warned this week that teenagers who fail online coolness tests develop serious health problems. Schools in several countries have already banned the whole game.
mainIdea.why: The article says psychologists are not worried. Nothing is banned, and no health problems appear.
